---
title: "Embedded web server"
---

fjåge uses Jetty 12.1's native HTTP and WebSocket APIs on Java 17. Groovy 5 applications can use the same APIs. Static content, file uploads, the web shell, observer streams, and remote-container WebSockets share a `WebServer` instance on each port.

## Handler structure

The server starts when `WebServer.getInstance(port)` is called. Contexts and rewrite rules can be added while it is running. A context starts before it becomes available to requests, and the context collection owns its lifecycle. Removing a context detaches it before stopping and destroying its handlers and resources. Lifecycle cleanup runs outside the collection lock, so it can manage dependent contexts.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Server --> CompressionHandler
    CompressionHandler --> RewriteHandler
    RewriteHandler --> Sequence
    Sequence --> ContextHandlerCollection
    Sequence --> DefaultHandler
    ContextHandlerCollection --> ResourceHandler
    ContextHandlerCollection --> UploadHandler
    ContextHandlerCollection --> WebSocketUpgradeHandler
```

Compression uses gzip for HTML, plain text, XML, CSS, and JavaScript. Static resources support welcome files, cache headers, ETags, HEAD requests, and byte ranges. A bare static context such as `/files` redirects to `/files/` with HTTP 302. Custom HTTP handlers and WebSocket contexts accept the bare context path directly.

## Migrating custom HTTP handlers from Jetty 9

`WebServer.addHandler()` now takes `org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler`. Replace subclasses of Jetty 9's `AbstractHandler` and the servlet request/response signature with `Handler.Abstract` and the native signature. Code that uses Jetty types must be migrated and recompiled, even when its imports have the same names. The servlet API is no longer supplied as a transitive dependency.

Before:

```java
server.addHandler("/hello", new AbstractHandler() {
  @Override
  public void handle(String target, Request baseRequest,
                     HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response) throws IOException {
    response.setContentType("text/plain;charset=utf-8");
    response.getWriter().print("hello");
    baseRequest.setHandled(true);
  }
});
```

After:

```java
import org.eclipse.jetty.http.HttpHeader;
import org.eclipse.jetty.io.Content;
import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler;
import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request;
import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Response;
import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback;

server.addHandler("/hello", new Handler.Abstract() {
  @Override
  public boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback) {
    response.getHeaders().put(HttpHeader.CONTENT_TYPE, "text/plain;charset=utf-8");
    Content.Sink.write(response, true, "hello", callback);
    return true;
  }
});
```

Return `false` to pass a request to the next handler, leaving its callback untouched. Return `true` when accepting a request and complete its callback exactly once, after the response write finishes or processing fails. Passing the callback to `Content.Sink.write()` or `Response.writeError()` lets Jetty complete it. Use `Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking` only when all work performed by the handler is nonblocking. Java 17 does not provide virtual threads.

Use `Request.getPathInContext(request)` for the path within a context and `request.getHeaders()` for HTTP headers. Replace servlet `sendError()` calls with `Response.writeError(request, response, callback, status)`. Custom `ErrorHandler` subclasses use the same native request/response/callback signature. The global and per-context `WebServer.setErrorHandler()` methods remain available.

Built-in rewrite rules such as `RewritePatternRule` remain supported through `WebServer.addRule()`. Custom `Rule` subclasses must implement Jetty 12's `matchAndApply(Rule.Handler)` API.

## WebSocket endpoints

`WebSocketServer` and `WebSocketHubConnector` retain their fjåge constructors and stream interfaces. They use native `WebSocketUpgradeHandler` contexts. To register a custom endpoint, call `WebServer.addWebSocket(context, creator, maxMsgSize)`. The creator uses Jetty 12's `ServerUpgradeRequest`, `ServerUpgradeResponse`, and HTTP `Callback` parameters.

Endpoints implement `org.eclipse.jetty.websocket.api.Session.Listener`. Store the session in `onWebSocketOpen()` and call `session.demand()` to receive an event. After processing a text message, demand the next event. Simple endpoints can implement `Session.Listener.AutoDemanding` instead. Send text with `session.sendText(text, websocketCallback)` and handle completion or failure through the WebSocket callback. The HTTP callback type and WebSocket callback type are different. Applications using Jetty's WebSocket client must declare `org.eclipse.jetty.websocket:jetty-websocket-jetty-client` themselves; fjåge tests use the JDK HTTP and WebSocket clients.

The fjåge endpoints extend Jetty's `Session.Listener.AbstractAutoDemanding`, which stores the session and automatically demands the next event after synchronous processing. A shared writer bridges the byte streams to ordered WebSocket text messages. The JDK UTF-8 decoder preserves characters split across writes and replaces malformed input.

The [buffer and line limits](java17.qmd#buffer-and-line-limits) bound accumulated stream data. Closing a connector is idempotent, and a late connection cannot reopen it. Each send has a two-second timeout; a timeout or failure disconnects the affected session. The configured maximum text-message size and long idle timeout remain in effect.

`waitOutputCompletion(timeout)` waits for output accepted before the call to finish sending. An unfinished line or UTF-8 character remains pending. The method returns `false` on timeout, interruption, or closure with unfinished output. Hub completion waits for each attempted send, including disconnection of failed peers. Completion does not acknowledge processing by the remote application.

## File uploads and directory listings

`WebServer.addUpload()` retains its overloads. Native multipart parsing enforces the configured maximum file size, request size, memory threshold, and temporary directory. The default upload limits remain 1 GiB per file and request, with a 100 MiB memory threshold. Jetty also applies its default limits of 100 parts per request and 8 KiB of headers per part. Zero or negative file/request size limits remain unlimited. An empty temporary-directory setting uses the JVM temporary directory.

Multipart parsing and file writes run as blocking work on Jetty worker threads. Uploaded filenames are URL-encoded before resolving them beneath the output directory. Successful uploads return the saved paths as UTF-8 plain text. Multipart failures return HTTP 400, unsupported methods return HTTP 405, and file-write failures return HTTP 500. Temporary multipart files are released on success, parsing failure, and disconnect.

Directory listing remains opt-in through `WebServerOptions.directoryListed(true)`. Requests with `Content-Type: text/plain` receive names, sizes, and timestamps; requests with `Content-Type: application/json` receive JSON entries. JSON filenames are escaped and hidden files are omitted. Other requests use Jetty's resource handler.

## Logging and packaging

Jetty logs through SLF4J. The packaged runtime uses `slf4j-jdk14` to send those logs to Java logging, with the `org.eclipse.jetty` category set to `WARNING`. Applications that supply another SLF4J provider should select a single provider for their runtime.

Use a clean build when upgrading to remove old Jetty and servlet JARs from `build/libs`:

```sh
./gradlew clean test loadTest jar javadoc
```

See Jetty's [HTTP programming guide](https://jetty.org/docs/jetty/12.1/programming-guide/server/http.html) and [WebSocket programming guide](https://jetty.org/docs/jetty/12.1/programming-guide/server/websocket.html) for the native APIs.
